title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 1 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 1)

content.overview: Section 1 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 states the Act's short title, territorial extent and commencement. It is an opening provision: it identifies the enactment and its temporal commencement, while the substantive arbitration mechanisms begin in the operative Parts and sections that follow.

sections.heading: Short title
sections.body: Section 1(1) provides that the enactment may be called the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The statutory title identifies the governing legislation and should be used precisely in pleadings and legal analysis.

sections.heading: Extent
sections.body: Section 1(2) states the territorial extent of the Act. The current India Code text must be used when addressing historical territorial provisos or adaptations; obsolete historical wording should not be treated as current law.

sections.heading: Commencement
sections.body: Section 1(3) provides that the Act comes into force on a date appointed by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette. India Code records 22 August 1996 as the enforcement date.

sections.heading: Analytical significance
sections.body: Section 1 is not the source of an arbitration agreement, arbitral jurisdiction, appointment power or award remedy. Those questions must be traced to the operative provisions of the Act. Section 1 instead establishes the statute's identity, territorial operation and commencement.

examples.title: Statutory application
examples.body: A pleading invoking arbitration legislation should identify the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 accurately and then cite the operative provision governing the relief sought. Section 1 supplies the enactment's formal identity; it does not itself confer the requested procedural remedy.

examples.title: Boundary case
examples.body: A party cannot rely on section 1 alone to establish that a court must appoint an arbitrator, refer a dispute, stay proceedings or enforce an award. The operative statutory provision for the particular procedural stage must be identified.

hypotheticals.question: What does section 1 establish when a dispute arises under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
hypotheticals.analysis: It establishes the short title, territorial extent and commencement framework. The substantive question must then be answered under the relevant operative provision of the Act.

hypotheticals.question: Can section 1 itself establish a party's entitlement to appointment of an arbitrator?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 1 is an opening provision concerning the Act's title, extent and commencement. Appointment entitlement must be traced to the applicable operative provision.

cases.name: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation
cases.facts: The Court considered arbitrability and the role of the referral court.
cases.issue: When should a court refer parties to arbitration and which disputes are non-arbitrable?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Referral scrutiny is limited, but the court must reject inherently non-arbitrable disputes and examine the arbitration agreement at the statutory threshold.
cases.holding: The Court formulated the modern Indian framework for arbitrability and referral.
cases.relevance: Use for arbitration agreement, referral and jurisdictional threshold questions.

cases.name: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd.
cases.facts: The dispute concerned unilateral appointment power vested in an interested party.
cases.issue: Whether a person interested in the outcome may unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator.
cases.ratioDecidendi: A person rendered ineligible to act as arbitrator cannot control the appointment process in a manner that creates justifiable bias.
cases.holding: The unilateral appointment mechanism was held invalid in the circumstances.
cases.relevance: Use for independence, impartiality and appointment challenges.

cases.name: Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. Cherian Varkey Construction Co. (P) Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined court-referred ADR under CPC s. 89.
cases.issue: How should courts select an appropriate ADR process?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The statutory ADR options must be applied according to the nature of the dispute and consent requirements.
cases.holding: The Court clarified the working scheme of CPC s. 89 and Order X.
cases.relevance: Use for mediation, conciliation and court-referred ADR.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the legal function of section 1 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 1 identifies the Act by short title, states its territorial extent and provides the commencement mechanism. It does not itself create an arbitration agreement or confer a specific procedural remedy.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The provision is foundational and must be read with the operative provisions that follow.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should section 1 be cited in an arbitration pleading?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Use section 1 to identify the governing enactment and its formal operation, then cite the precise substantive or procedural provision that creates the right, power or remedy in issue.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: This prevents an opening provision from being used as a substitute for the operative statutory rule.
